newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US trade gap balloon seen pricked in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US trade gap balloon seen pricked in Feb.

text.p: With aircraft exports up and oil prices down, the U.S. international trade deficit probably narrowed in February after ballooning unexpectedly to $12.71 billion in January, economists said.

"Customs receipts indicate a small decline in imports while the shipments data indicate an increase in exports, so that should give us the narrowing we are looking for," said Sandy Battan, international economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A., who predicted a $10.0 billion gap in February.
The Commerce Department is scheduled to release the report on Thursday, April 17, at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Wall Street economists polled by Reuters called for the February trade deficit to shrink to $10.1 billion from January's $12.71 billion -- its highest level in more than nine years.

Economists said January's figure was "unsustainable". They attributed the soaring gap to higher oil prices and record imports of industrial supplies and materials, capital goods, autos and auotmobile parts. Also, U.S.-produced commercial aircraft exports plummeted to their lowest level in a year.
"We are looking for a $10 billion deficit -- a decline from January's figure that was rather erratically strong," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A.

However, some economists predicted a continuation of January's trend in February. They argued that a strong dollar and less-buoyant foreign markets limited U.S. exports while a robust U.S. economy drew in rising imports.

"What you are seeing in the first quarter is the strong dollar finally having a really large impact on the export side," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc, who forecast a February deficit of $13.5 billion.
"The other thing is the U.S. domestic economy is very strong right now, especially retail demand, and we are selling a lot of imports. That makes the trade deficit look that much worse," Low added.
The trade figures will spur analysts to fine tune their gross domestic product (GDP) forecasts for the first quarter, but major revisions are unlikely if the data meets expectations, analysts said.
"I don't think a $10 billion February trade deficit would justify pushing GDP forecasts over four percent," Sloan said.
"I think some people don't seem to have fully taken into account the (January) trade deterioration in making their first quarter GDP forecasts," he added.

Economists interviewed saw the U.S. bilateral trade deficit with Japan unchanged to slightly wider in February. The politically sensitive U.S. gap with Japan edged higher by 0.7 percent to $4.29 billion in January, falling short of the markets' worst fears.
The dollar will be bolstered if the trade forecasts are met while the Treasury market reaction will likely be muted regardless of the outcome of the data, economists said.
"The Federal Reserve is focusing on the domestic economy and because of that the (Treasury) market might be skeptical that trade is all that important," HSBC's Low said.
A less-than-expected narrowing or rise in the February overall trade gap or bilateral deficit with Japan could put a short-lived dent in the dollar, economists said.

"The trade figures might make the dollar wobble a little bit, but I don't think it will be able to outweigh the lift from other factors," said Citicorp's Batten, referring to prospects for growing interest rate differentials between the United States and most of Europe and Japan.
